title: The month of Katak
hookLine: in Katak we reap what we did; blame no one else (Barah Maha, ang 135)

cards: A dent appears on the family car. Nobody did it. Not the kids, not the spouse; the neighbor's teenager is the obvious suspect, and the shopping cart in the parking lot a close second.
Everyone has a story, and in every story the dent happened to them. It's an old habit: when something goes wrong, the first thing the mind builds is an alibi.
Katak falls roughly from mid-October to mid-November, the season when the crops that were sown come in. And Guru Arjan's Katak stanza opens with a line that takes the alibi apart.

teach.h: KARAM KAMAAVANE: WE EARN OUR DEEDS.
teach.b: It begins katak karam kamaavane, dos na kaahoo jog. In paraphrase: in Katak, we earn what our deeds earn; no one else is to be blamed. Karam here is deeds, what you've actually done.

Kamaavane is the everyday Punjabi word for earning, the way you earn wages. Dos is fault, blame. It's almost a farmer's line: what you planted is what's in the field, so there's no point shouting at the neighbor's crop.
Then the stanza says where the trouble really starts.
Forgetting the Lord, every illness takes hold. Turning your face away, you're separated, life after life. The world's pleasures turn bitter in an instant.
So the deepest deed in the stanza isn't stealing or lying. It's forgetting. This isn't a stanza of doom.
Sikh teaching holds deeds and grace together: you reap what you sow, and the Guru's mercy can still reach the field.
And the stanza ends with the way out: in Katak, in the company of the holy, all worries fall away.
Notice what owning a fault does. While you're busy blaming, you're stuck, because only the other person can fix it.

The moment you say, that one was mine, you can apologize, repair, plant differently. Blaming no one isn't blaming yourself harshly. It's simply standing in your own field, honestly, and starting from there.
Diwali, and with it the Sikh Bandi Chhor Divas, usually falls in this season of harvest: a festival of lamps for a month about seeing clearly.

how: On the Sangrand of Katak, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Katak stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha; it is heard as a call to take responsibility for their deeds while trusting in the Guru's grace.

o: a festival day when grudges are set aside
a lamp lit to remember the Guru's release
the harvest month of owning your own deeds

games.q: the month of Katak — tap the pairs.

s: the Katak stanza names forgetting the Lord as where the trouble starts
forgetting, it says, lets every illness take hold.
blaming no one means blaming yourself harshly
it means standing honestly in your own field so you can repair it.
the stanza ends in doom with no way out
it ends: in the company of the holy, all worries fall away.

games.q: something has gone wrong and everyone is pointing fingers. what does the Katak stanza say?
o: find out who's really at fault and tell them.
we earn what our deeds earn; blame no one else.
it was fate, so nobody needs to do anything.
games.why: katak karam kamaavane, dos na kaahoo jog: our own deeds bring the harvest, and no one else is to blame. owning it is what lets you repair it.

practice: Look back over the week for one small thing that went wrong where you'd been telling a story about someone else: a missed message, a sharp reply, a forgotten promise.
Without punishing yourself, say inwardly, that part was mine, and notice how it feels to set the alibi down, and what small repair it opens. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Katak. In the Barah Maha, Katak is the honest month: we earn what our deeds earn, no one else is to blame, and the holy company lifts the worry.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: karam, deeds. In Gurbani the word can also mean grace, from a Persian word for generosity.

carryVoice: Your line: katak: blame no one. Owning a fault is where mending starts. See you in Maghar.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, the Katak stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135)
